extraction.name: SWE-Gym
extraction.description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. It contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. It is designed to bridge the gap in suitable training environments for language model-based SWE agents, which require interaction with an executable runtime, appropriate software dependencies, and reproducible test suites.
extraction.creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
extraction.citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang. Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym comprises 2,438 real-world software engineering tasks sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. These tasks include pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases, constructed in close alignment with SWE-Bench. The process involved identifying repositories using SEART GitHub search, extracting task instances using SWE-Bench's script, versioning instances, and manually configuring dependencies for each task instance. This manual configuration and validation process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours. A subset of 230 tasks, SWE-Gym Lite, was also identified for rapid prototyping by filtering out tasks requiring editing more than one file, poorly described problem statements, excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation. Additionally, SWE-Gym Raw, a larger set of 64,689 Python GitHub issues without executable environments, was collected from 358 Python repositories.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world software engineering tasks from GitHub issues and pull requests in 11 popular open-source Python repositories. SWE-Gym Raw contains 64,689 task instances from 358 Python repositories.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For SWE-Gym Lite, tasks were filtered to exclude those requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The collected GitHub issues were converted into task instances using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. Each instance includes a natural language description of the issue, a snapshot of the repository, and a set of unit tests. Executable environments were set up by semi-automatically collecting version numbers and manually configuring dependencies for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. Instances were then validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code, and failed instances were filtered out.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The process of setting up executable environments and verifying instances involved manual configuration of dependencies for each task instance. This was done by human annotators using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. The SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was then used to ensure that the gold patch (human-submitted code diff) passed more unit tests than the original code.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The validation process filtered out failed instances, resulting in 2,438 unit-test-validated instances. This implies an analysis of whether the gold patch successfully resolved the issue based on unit test outcomes.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: A subset of the authors performed the annotations.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: To facilitate further research, SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories are publicly released. For full reproducibility, pre-built Docker images for each instance, totaling 6 TB, are publicly released.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries, potentially supporting critical open-source infrastructure and making software development more accessible. However, as these agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Additionally, similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. Future work is encouraged to explore frameworks for responsible deployment, including security, safety, and economic impacts.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The data collection process for SWE-Gym Lite introduces a bias by excluding tasks that require editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation. The distribution of tasks across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of the total tasks, while bokeh represents only one percent. Repeated sampling for self-improvement experiments shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, biasing the training towards easier tasks if not mitigated by per-instance capping.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories, types of tasks, and programming languages. The current size and repository diversity are not yet performance bottlenecks, suggesting that further improvements could be achieved by allocating more computing resources to sampling more training trajectories. The gap between Pass@k and Best@k metrics indicates imperfect performance of the trained verifier, suggesting room for improvements in reward modeling for coding agents. Self-improvement results are modest, and more advanced policy optimization methods or stronger base models might be needed. The current SWE settings focus solely on task completion, neglecting human-in-the-loop collaboration, which is essential for real-world software engineering.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. SWE-Gym is used for training language model-based SWE agents and verifiers. It supports training state-of-the-art open-weight SWE agents and training verifier models to enable inference-time scaling. It is also used for self-improvement experiments with specialized workflow agents. The dataset is used for evaluating agent performance on SWE-Bench Lite and Verified benchmarks. Usage Guidelines: The dataset is intended to facilitate research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis. For full reproducibility, pre-built Docker images for each instance are publicly released.
